limitations: Theorem 1.1 and its corollaries are taken from the delivered manuscript as reported; the finite-field rank-layer estimates in Sections 4-7 were not independently verified here.

Lovasz's local radii, Coregliano's degree-count thresholds, Conlon-Lee's reflection-group results, Im-Li-Liu's subdivision results and the original KNRS paper are known here only through abstracts or through the counterexample's citations, not from delivered full texts.

Several neighbouring lines (tournament and digraph analogues, hypergraph Sidorenko exponents, spectral Sidorenko inequalities) are inventoried but not delivered, so the standard does not rank questions in those lines.
The Lean formalization and the small-graph computations named in the field description are not in the inventory, so the standard treats them as unsupported until delivered.

The standard rests on extracted text from PDFs in which some formulas are garbled; theorem statements were read from the surrounding prose and numbering, and a statement under review may be asked to quote the exact hypothesis it relies on.

objections.claim: The field description's assertion that a Lean formalization covers the Sidorenko statement is unsupported by any delivered or inventoried source.
objections.reason: An inventory query for 'Lean' returned zero items, and the delivered counterexample manuscript makes no mention of a formalization; the bar therefore treats the refutation as a reported manuscript result, and any statement that leans on a formal verification must supply it.
objections.resolution_condition: Delivery of the Lean artifact together with the exact statement it formalizes (graph versus kernel form; homomorphism versus injective counts; whether the finite host is constructed or only shown to exist), so that the formal coverage can be matched against Theorem 1.1, Corollary 1.2 and Corollary 1.3.

objections.claim: Theorem 1.1 of the counterexample manuscript is accepted here as reported, not as verified; the bar's premises about what is refuted depend on it.
objections.reason: The proof reduces Theorem 1.1 to Lemma 3.1, whose proof occupies Sections 4-7 and requires a fixed even dimension above an unstated threshold (and D > 1641 for the singular nondirect case) before q tends to infinity; the host is produced only by existence (Lemma 3.6); no independent verification was delivered. The manuscript's own consistency checks (compatibility with Lovasz's local results, exclusion from every positive class) are internal and do not substitute for verification.
objections.resolution_condition: Delivery of an independent check of Lemma 3.1 and Lemma 3.6 (a refereed version, a formal verification, or an explicit finite host with computed densities), or a statement under review that explicitly conditions its premises on the manuscript.

objections.claim: No delivered source contains the 'computations on small graphs' named in the field description; the only attested smallest open case is K_{5,5} minus C_{10}.
objections.reason: Hatami (2008) names K_{5,5} minus a Hamiltonian cycle as the smallest graph for which the conjecture is open; the SOS paper and the convex-graphon-parameters paper treat it as still open and not weakly norming; nothing delivered enumerates small bipartite graphs or gives numerical evidence, so a statement that rests a conjecture on such computations must supply them.
objections.resolution_condition: Delivery of the computational source (enumeration range, method, and the graphs certified or left open), so that a statement's appeal to small-graph evidence can be checked against it.

value.consequence: The standard is fixed on the delivered sources. The field is no longer 'prove Sidorenko's conjecture' but the characterization and replacement problem left by the reported 2026 counterexample (incidence graph of 22 triples on 13 points; 35 vertices, 66 edges; Theorem 1.1 gives a finite simple host with t(H,G) < p(G)^66; Corollary 1.2 amplifies the deficit by tensor powers and gives a fixed injective-copy deficit at positive density under balanced blow-ups; Corollary 1.3 refutes the forcing conjecture at one density and does not assert failure at every density; the paper itself locates the example outside every delivered positive class and inside no local-Sidorenko neighbourhood). A statement graded against this bar must place its question by an explicit reduction or implication into one of the lines named below, must state what the counterexample does and does not settle for that question (one density versus all densities; homomorphism versus injective counts; graph versus kernel; the example's irregular point side and connectedness), must compare against the named neighbours (K_{5,5} minus C_{10} and C_6 box K_2; the forcing replacement; KNRS and regular-KNRS status of the counterexample; the Sidorenko exponent and the blow-up/L^p threshold; symmetric patterns; the local radius), and must answer the strongest objection in this field, which is that a question about one more bipartite graph or one more triple system is a parameter increment without a new mechanism. Missing decisive sources and unsupported inferences are listed in the objections and limitations.
value.reason: FIRST, the field and its active lines. The field is homomorphism-density inequalities t(H,.) >= t(K_2,.)^{e(H)} for bipartite H over graphs, kernels and graphons, with the forcing, local Sidorenko and Kohayakawa-Nagle-Rodl-Schacht (KNRS) relatives. The organizing event is the delivered manuscript 'A counterexample to Sidorenko's conjecture' (September 23, 2026): H is the incidence graph of the 22 faces on 13 points of Table 1, parts of sizes 13 and 22, degrees 4, 5, 6 on the point side and 3 on the face side, connected, every point pair in exactly two faces; Theorem 1.1 asserts a finite simple G with t(H,G) < p(G)^66, proved by a finite-field rank-layer kernel (symmetric matrices over F_q of even dimension D, half-rank layers with prescribed discriminant sign), a negative four-incidence correlation forced by the double occurrence of pairs, a type-pinning step by colour refinement that is discrete within each part (Proposition 2.1(4), Lemma 3.4), dilution and a crossed product to a symmetric kernel, and sampling to a finite host (Lemma 3.6); Sections 4-7 prove the rank-layer limit (Lemma 3.1) with D fixed large (the singular-contribution bound needs D > 1641) before q tends to infinity. Corollary 1.2: tensor powers make t(H,F)/p(F)^66 arbitrarily small, and balanced blow-ups give Inj(H,F_s) <= (1 - delta)(n_s)_{35} d_s^66 at a positive limiting density, contradicting the Erdos-Simonovits injective benchmark of CFS Section 1. Corollary 1.3: a nonconstant graphon W with t(K_2,W) = p, t(H,W) = p^66 and t(C_4,W) > p^4, so H is not p-forcing at one density and the forcing conjecture (CFS Conjecture 2: bipartite with a cycle iff forcing) is false; the manuscript explicitly does not assert failure at every density. The manuscript itself records that H has no vertex complete to the other part (so CFS Theorem 1.2 does not apply), is not weakly norming (Hatami Theorem 2.10(ii) requires equal degrees within a part), fails Coregliano's degree-count hypothesis in both orientations, has minimum degree 3 so is not an even-path substitution, and that its mean-one kernel lies outside Lovasz's local neighbourhoods (sup-norm radius 1/(4m), cut-norm radius 2^{-8m-2}). The active lines, with the delivered works that show them: (1) positive classes by gluing and entropy: Li-Szegedy logarithmic calculus (also forcing for one vertex complete to the other side); Szegedy's information-theoretic approach with topological conditions and a hypergraph extension; Kim-Lee-Lee tree-arrangeable graphs and T box H; Conlon-Kim-Lee-Lee strongly tree-decomposable graphs, subdivisions of graphs satisfying a KNRS-type locally dense counting hypothesis (Theorem 3.1, K_{2,t}-replacements, Problem 1.5 asking for subdivisions of arbitrary graphs), and H box C_{2k}; the higher-tree-decomposition note; Coregliano-Razborov reflective tree decompositions and the elementary biregular-host reduction; CFS Theorem 1.1 (comparison with K_{r,d}) and Corollary 1.1 (t(H,G) >= p^{m+w} with w the width). (2) Graph norms and domination: Hatami's Holder/weakly Holder characterization (Theorem 2.8), positive classes (Theorem 2.9: biproducts, K_{m,n}, hypercubes), necessary conditions (Theorem 2.10), and open questions including K_{5,5} minus a Hamilton cycle as the smallest open case; Kral'-Martins-Pach-Wrochna step Sidorenko property and an edge-transitive bipartite graph that is not weakly norming; Sidorenko's theorem that weakly norming graphs are edge-transitive; Lee-Schulke convex graphon parameters showing K_{5,5} minus C_{10} and C_6 box K_2 are not weakly norming; Lee's factorisation and non-uniform-convexity remarks; Conlon-Lee domination; the cyclic-amalgam strong-domination family; the fold-stability characterization of cut-percolation. (3) Blow-ups and L^p versions: Conlon-Lee divisibility and degree-count criteria, every H has a Sidorenko one-sided blow-up, equivalently an L^p Sidorenko inequality for some p; Coregliano's left-cut-percolation and induced-Sidorenko bigraphs. (4) Forcing: CFS Conjecture 2 and Theorem 1.3; the adjunction/box-product forcing-family paper (balanced blow-ups, subdivisions, Cartesian and strong products); Corollary 1.3 of the counterexample. (5) KNRS and locally dense hosts: Bradac-Sudakov-Wigderson (gluing H_1 ltimes H_2 preserves KNRS, Conjecture 1.6 KNRS-forcing, Conjecture 1.8 regular-KNRS, Lemma 2.6 graphon equivalences, Corollary 2.15 W - p is PSD for regular locally dense W, hereditarily PSD-nonnegative graphs, Proposition 5.1 obstructions to tensoring and operator powers without regularity, Proposition 5.2 a graph that is not PSD-nonnegative); KNRS for subdivisions; the L^p form of KNRS; the tensor-amplification/spectral-transfer framework. (6) Local Sidorenko: Lovasz's signed-graphon results. (7) Proof-system obstructions: no sum-of-squares certificate for the smallest open case and for odd Blakley-Roy. (8) Host reductions and special hosts: Coregliano-Razborov biregularity; Zhao's conjugacy-class averaging reduction; Csikvari-Lin for colourings, independent sets and Widom-Rowlinson hosts. (9) Analogues: Fox-Pham-Zhao characterize common and Sidorenko linear equations; the reverse Sidorenko inequality; hypergraph Sidorenko is false (Sidorenko 1993, recorded in CFS); tournament and digraph analogues are inventoried but not delivered. SECOND, the nearest known problems and what a resolution would give. P1 (characterization): determine the class S of bipartite graphs with the Sidorenko property; sub-questions with fixed resolution conditions are the status of K_{5,5} minus C_{10} and C_6 box K_2 (smallest open per Hatami; not weakly norming; no SOS certificate), the minimum order and size of a counterexample, closure of S under subdivision (CKLL Problem 1.5 now has the subdivision of the counterexample as a test), and decidability of membership (CFS raise undecidability by analogy with Hatami-Norine). A resolution replaces a refuted universal statement with a boundary; nothing delivered gives any necessary condition for membership in S beyond bipartiteness. P2 (symmetric patterns): is every biregular, edge-transitive or vertex-transitive bipartite graph Sidorenko? Documented distinction: the counterexample's pinning (Lemma 3.4) needs colour refinement from the part colours to become discrete within each part, which fails for any biregular H, so the only known negative mechanism does not reach biregular patterns; on the positive side, weakly norming implies edge-transitive (Sidorenko) but edge-transitive does not imply weakly norming (step-Sidorenko paper), and Hatami's necessary conditions require part-regularity, so the symmetric classes are not covered by the norming route either; Coregliano-Razborov reduce hosts, not patterns, to biregular. P3 (forcing replacement): the forcing conjecture is false; open are whether 'bipartite with a cycle and Sidorenko' implies forcing, whether failure of p-forcing at one density implies failure at all densities, and the stability statement for the positive classes (CFS Theorem 1.3, Li-Szegedy, forcing families). P4 (quantitative replacement): the Sidorenko exponent s(H) = inf{s : t(H,G) >= p(G)^s for all G}; CFS give s(H) <= e(H) + w(H); Corollary 1.2(i) gives s(H) > 66 for the counterexample; determine s(H) there and whether s(H) - e(H) is controlled by a structural parameter; relatedly the minimal blow-up/L^p exponent of Conlon-Lee for the counterexample. P5 (KNRS status of the counterexample): by BSW Lemma 2.6, H is KNRS iff t(H,W) >= p^{e(H)} for every p-locally dense W, and Sidorenko hosts need not be locally dense, so whether the counterexample H is KNRS, regular-KNRS (Conjecture 1.8), or hereditarily PSD-nonnegative is open; a resolution decides whether local density (or regularity plus local density, where W - p is PSD) is the right replacement hypothesis, and whether KNRS for bipartite H is equivalent to Sidorenko. P6 (local radius): Lovasz's radii depend on m; whether the constant graphon is a strict local minimizer in cut distance with a radius of better m-dependence, and how the counterexample kernel sits relative to that radius; connects to the PSD viewpoint of BSW and the equality-case regularization in the tensor-amplification abstract. P7 (obstruction theorem): a checkable necessary condition for S, generalizing the double-occurrence negative correlation; and whether the entropy/gluing, norming and blow-up methods are jointly complete for S. P8 (proof systems): extend the SOS obstruction to the counterexample's inequality and to the positive classes. THIRD, what counts as a substantial advance: a result that changes what specialists do next, namely (a) a necessary condition for S, or a second counterexample with a different mechanism or materially smaller order, with the mechanism isolated; (b) resolution of P2 for a named symmetric class in either direction; (c) a theorem tying Sidorenko to forcing, to KNRS or regular-KNRS, or to local minimality for cyclic bipartite graphs, i.e. a replacement conjecture with a proved implication in one direction; (d) decidability or undecidability of S; (e) s(H) for the counterexample or a bound beating the width bound in general; (f) the status of K_{5,5} minus C_{10}; (g) a positive method whose reach is proved to exceed entropy gluing, norming and blow-ups by a documented exclusion. Not substantial: adding a graph to a positive class by an existing gluing rule; a second triple system fed to the same construction without new mechanism; restating Corollaries 1.2-1.3. FOURTH, the specialist's meaning of levels 2 and 3. Ground B1 (standing), level 2: the question is placed by an explicit implication or reduction inside one of P1-P8 (for instance: 'if H' is Sidorenko then CKLL Theorem 1.3(ii) gives its subdivision; if biregular graphs are Sidorenko then Coregliano-Razborov's biregular reduction plus X gives Y'), the premises are verified against the delivered statements (the exact hypotheses of CFS Theorem 1.1, Hatami Theorem 2.10, Conlon-Lee's criteria, Lovasz's radii, Corollary 1.3's single-density quantifier), the strongest objection (the conjecture is already refuted, so one more instance settles nothing) is answered by saying what the instance decides for the line, and the remaining uncertainty (including dependence on the unverified counterexample proof) is explicit; shared vocabulary ('Sidorenko-type') is not a connection. Level 3: additionally a demonstrated or compellingly argued account that the resolution removes an obstacle the line is stuck on, with an explanation of why existing results and nearby alternatives do not already provide it, e.g. that neither the delivered positive methods nor the colour-refinement pinning reach biregular patterns, or that the width bound and blow-up thresholds leave s(H) undetermined by a documented gap. Ground B2 (influence), level 2: the carrying criterion is met concretely: named results that become unconditional (Ramsey multiplicity for the class, CFS Section 3; forcing or stability for the class via CFS Theorem 1.3 or Li-Szegedy; subdivision and product closures via CKLL and the forcing-families paper), or the competing mechanisms distinguished (gluing-type positivity versus double-occurrence negative correlation; local density versus edge density; homomorphism versus injective), or a delimited limitation of a named method (SOS, entropy gluing, norming, colour-refinement pinning), or implications under each answer, with the argued part saying why that change matters. Level 3: a compellingly argued account that the answer changes the organizing explanation, e.g. a structural criterion for S, an undecidability theorem, or a proved equivalence between Sidorenko and forcing or KNRS for cyclic bipartite graphs, with the reason existing results do not already yield it. Comparative priority, level 2: the question is compared by payoff with the credible neighbours listed above (K_{5,5} minus C_{10}; C_6 box K_2; the subdivision of the counterexample; one density versus all densities in forcing; KNRS versus regular-KNRS versus PSD-nonnegativity of the counterexample; s(H) versus the L^p threshold; biregular versus edge-transitive versus vertex-transitive; sup-norm versus cut-norm local radius), and the strongest relevant objection is answered: typically 'a parameter increment without a new mechanism' or 'the general obstruction theorem is the better question'. Level 3: a concrete advantage of the chosen formulation is supported by documented distinctions from the sources, such as the pinning step's need for discrete refinement, BSW's PSD structure for regular locally dense graphons, Conlon-Lee's eventual blow-up positivity, or Lovasz's explicit radii; a neighbour's settledness alone does not establish superiority. FIFTH, what makes a question uninteresting here: restating Sidorenko's conjecture or asking whether it is true; asking about a graph already inside a delivered positive class; varying the triple system or the dimension and prime in the delivered construction without a new mechanism; a conjecture resting only on small-graph enumeration (no such enumeration was delivered in any case); a 'programme' to understand the Sidorenko property without a resolution condition; hypergraph Sidorenko (false since 1993) or Sidorenko linear equations (characterized by Fox-Pham-Zhao); forcing questions that do not fix the density quantifier; questions already answered by Lovasz's local results, by Corollaries 1.2-1.3, or by Hatami's necessary conditions. Absence of a route to progress is not a reason against a question whose significance case reaches level 3, and absence of downstream theorems is not a reason against a question whose explanatory payoff is the significance. Missing decisive sources and unsupported inferences: the Lean formalization named in the field description is absent from the inventory (query 'Lean' returned nothing) and nothing delivered verifies it; no source of small-graph computations was delivered; the counterexample's Theorem 1.1 is reported, not independently verified here, and its proof rests on Lemma 3.1 with a large fixed dimension and an existence-only host; Lovasz's radii and Coregliano's degree-count thresholds are known to me only through the counterexample's citations and the delivered abstracts; the Conlon-Lee reflection-group paper, Im-Li-Liu, the original KNRS paper and the tournament analogues were not delivered and no claim here depends on their content.
